title: Power of 2
subtitle: How to Make the Most of Your Partnerships at Work and in Life
author: Rodd Wagner & Gale Muller
note: On the importance of having a counterweight when you're developing something difficult, whether that's a business or a new technology.

title: Handmade
subtitle: A Scientist's Search for Meaning through Making
author: Anna Ploszajski
note: A journey through materials by way of the craft of making them. A materials engineer's job is often translating an idea between the computer and reality, and this book really brings that home.

title: Pluto's Republic
author: Peter Medawar
note: A collection of essays that gave me a real scepticism of systems and bureaucracies: a group of clever people can do stupid things through no individual's fault.

title: The Art of the Soluble
author: Peter Medawar
note: Knowing which problem to solve is as important as solving it. Medawar really shaped my thinking that a good scientist knows where to spend their efforts. My copy is the one collected in Pluto's Republic.

title: Rebel Ideas
subtitle: The Power of Diverse Thinking
author: Matthew Syed
note: Why diversity of thought is critical to solving hard problems.

title: What Money Can't Buy
subtitle: The Moral Limits of Markets
author: Michael Sandel
note: How money can crowd out norms that used to matter more, and why you should be careful when you change the way people see something.

title: Incognito
subtitle: The Secret Lives of the Brain
author: David Eagleman
note: I'm fascinated by how the brain solves problems, and this book taught me that most of our behaviour is driven by the unconscious mind.

title: Success through Failure
subtitle: The Paradox of Design
author: Henry Petroski
note: This book taught me that design is Janus-faced, always looking both backwards and forwards: designers must learn from past mistakes while planning future projects. History holds failures driven by ignorance, overconfidence and hubris.

title: The Social Control of Technology
author: David Collingridge
note: The basis for several of my articles. Collingridge examines why societies struggle to steer emerging technologies before their harmful effects develop.

title: I Wish I'd Made You Angry Earlier
subtitle: Essays on Science, Scientists, and Humanity
author: Max Perutz
note: An interesting walk through scientific discovery: sometimes an emotional reaction can trigger the focus needed for a solution. It's also where I learnt about Project Habbakuk.

title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
author: Eric S. Raymond
note: Top-down versus bottom-up approaches to software development apply to scientific discovery too. I use that as a key theme in my essays, and this is where the ideas started.
